The longtime NFL QB and former NC State legend could energize the Wolfpack fans and donors and provide an injection of NIL funding

        Former NC State standout quarterback Philip Rivers has risen to the top of the Wolfpack's coaching search, according to industry sources, following Saturday's firing of veteran Dave Doeren in his 14th season at the program.Rivers, whose four-star quarterback son Gunner is committed to the Wolfpack for 2027, has coached St. Michael Catholic High (Fairhope, Alabama) since the 2021 season, which included his brief NFL return to the Indianapolis Colts for a cup of tea near the end of the 2025 campaign.Rivers sat down this week with NFL insider Daniel Jeremiah to discuss what he's learned on the sideline, oddly enough, shortly before news of NC State's coaching vacancy and his reported connection to it."It's blocking and tackling and catching and not turning the ball over at every level," Rivers said. "I know there are degrees to it, and I miss some of that high-level ball, but at the end of the day you watch on Friday nights, Saturdays and Sundays and it's who blocks and tackles the best and who protected the football. That's usually who wins."
It would take a substantial leap of faith from NC State's power brass and top-end boosters to believe Rivers, someone without college coaching experience, could take the Wolfpack to the next level. Rivers did interview for the Buffalo Bills' vacancy earlier this year, an opportunity many believe will assist him should a college opportunity -- like NC State -- arise."The thing I kept telling myself was be yourself," Rivers said of his NFL coaching interview. "I showed up in a golf shirt, khakis and some boots with a notebook in my arm."Rivers, who was not asked about NC State during this week's interview, said he's had to curtail some of his expectations at the prep level as a football-only guy.
"I think the biggest thing is the one way I've grown is understanding that not everybody is going to love the game like you do or like the guys at the level I was at do," Rivers said. "These are high school football players, high school students, who many are going onto Auburn and Alabama and Ole Miss and LSU as students and their last snap is here with us."For me, it's been, yeah, we want to win, but make sure you know the greater mission that you give them something more than run a slant, or pick up strong dogs or all the things we're teaching them. They better pick up more than that. Knowing for the masses it's bigger than just the Xs and Os."Rivers said he watches as much football as he can with his sons, including Gunner, one of the top signal callers in this year's recruiting cycle.
"I came down here (to Alabama) with the Colts and Chargers' playbooks, just ready to go for it, and you find out real quick you have to scale it back a little bit," Rivers said. "At the same time, the guys loved being challenged and then showing a clip of Jonathan Taylor running outside zone and us calling it the same thing."Where NC State standsMoving on from Doeren was a necessary decision after the program failed to progress this fall, despite high preseason expectations and a favorable ACC slate. NC State invested considerable resources this offseason by going all-in on quarterback CJ Bailey, which led to the loss of several other starters to the transfer portal.Credited with constructing the current roster, general manager Andy Vaughn was also fired following Friday night's loss at Stanford.
Signing a proper general manager at a school that doesn't spend as much on players as some of the others at the top of the conference will be pivotal and go hand in hand with this coaching search.Next season's expected 24-team expanded playoff benefits the Power Four's mid-tier, like NC State, which will have a shot at reaching the bracket annually with the right leader in a league not graced with multiple juggernauts.

body:
With BYU and Texas Tech tumbling, Devon Dampier took over in the second half to keep the Utes unbeaten and establish them as the Big 12's most complete team
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 25, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:57 am ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Warning signs came down the pipe for No. 10 Utah all day. First, rival No. 2 BYU fell on the road against UCF. Then, reigning Big 12 champion No. 8 Texas Tech dropped a miserable performance against Cincinnati. Entering Utah's kickoff against No. 14 Houston, there were only three undefeated teams remaining in college football: Miami, UCLA and the Utes. But through a half, Utah had to work through their inexperience. The Utes were held scoreless in the first half and had more three-and-outs (two) than red zone trips (one). But in the second half of a 21-13 victory, Utah wrestled away control of the postseason race and made their case as the Big 12's most complete team. After going down 10-0 halfway through the third quarter, Utah only needed a moment to collect itself. Quarterback Devon Dampier recorded 75 yards on five plays all by himself -- two passes and three runs -- to finally get on the board in only 2:21. 
The next drive, Utah reached Houston territory behind Dampier's arm, but added key runs from Daniel Bray and Wayshawn Parker to finally set up a five-yard touchdown run for the first lead of the game. When it was time to put the game away, Utah sent a sneaky blitz that confused Houston quarterback Conner Weigman and led to a strip-sack deep in Houston territory. Dampier was again able to get in the end zone, and the Utes' defense bowed up at the right moments to end the game. More than just the final stats, Utah's game control really stood apart. According to Game on Paper, 59% of their plays were successful, which ranks in the 96th percentile. They were especially good on rushes, ranking in the 93rd percentile. Even while missing a key offensive lineman and replacing all five offensive linemen from last season, results are still strong. 
Now, Utah holds a 13-game winning streak, the longest active streak at the FBS level. Even after the win, Utah is likely to remain behind BYU as the top-ranked Big 12 squad. The Cougars still have a historic win over No. 2 Notre Dame to fall back on, along with a win over Arizona that continues to age well. The Utes should easily jump Texas Tech and threaten an AP Top 5 ranking. The Utes still play BYU and Arizona in the coming weeks, but the dramatic win over Houston means Utah can afford to split the games and remain in the Big 12 title race. After ranking as perhaps the best two-loss team in America last season, though, there's plenty of urgency to get it right this time. Especially after losing three straight to the rival Cougars, finally getting the team in Salt Lake City is top priority. 
Utah was expected to set a new standard for the Big 12 when they moved from the Pac-12. It took two years and a coaching change, but the Utes are finally ascending to the head of the class.

body:
Brown says he has 'no beef' with former Celtics teammate Jayson Tatum, but how about a 'lamb chop?'

        Jaylen Brown is not going to let this Jayson Tatum beef die. Actually, it's not a beef. Let's make sure we get this correct. It's a ... lamb chop? Yes, a lamb chop. And some gravy. I can't believe I am writing this, but these were actual words spoken by Brown after the 76ers' win over the Bucks on Saturday night. "There's no beef," Brown said of his relationship with Tatum, his longtime Celtics teammate before a stunning offseason trade shipped him to rival Philadelphia. "Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. It's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chop. And some gravy. He should stay ready at all times."These are shots at Tatum. No two ways about it. He's got a great PR team? He should stay ready at all times? Brown sounds like he's in the middle of crafting a diss track. Personally, I can't wait for the next bar. This is high hoops drama. And if you're like me, you're praying to the basketball gods that we get a 76ers-Celtics playoff series. 
If you need a refresher on how we've arrived at this place in the Brown-Tatum beef ... er, lamb chop ... let's run through it. We'll call this the appetizer portion. Forgive me. I had to say it. 
It all started, of course, with Brown being traded to the 76ers. He wasn't happy about it. He's been playing the Rodney Dangerfield "I get no respect" card for years. He basically turned last season into an "I'm the best two-way player in the world" campaign tour while Tatum was sidelined with an Achilles tear. He hears every slight. And the Celtics trading him, in his eyes, was the biggest one yet, particularly on the heels of the best individual season of his life, one in which he led Boston to 56 wins and the East's No. 2 seed while Tatum rehabbed his injury. So he was ticked about the trade itself (which is understandable), and, perhaps even more so, by the way it was handled by the Celtics. He's never really elaborated on that other than to say there was a "lack of respect" and that "maybe one day we'll share the details of how everything transpired and all the moving parts that took place in this." 
        
            
                Jayson Tatum shuts down Jaylen Brown drama: 'This ain't f---in' Shaq and Kobe, there's no beef'
                
                    Robby Kalland                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
These were quotes from Brown's introductory press conference in Philadelphia. It was here that he was asked whether he and Tatum had talked following the trade. "Nah, not really," Brown said, and let's just say he didn't sound friendly about it. 
Fast forward to this past Thursday, when the latest episode of Tatum's documentary series, "Summer of Jayson," was released. In it, he detailed his reaction to learning of the Brown trade. Tatum said he was in Las Vegas when it went down. He had just come off the court from a workout when Celtics player development coach God Shammgod Jr. broke the news to him. "[Shammgod] handed me a towel," Tatum said. "He was like, 'Yo, put this over your face. Don't react. They just traded him.' I'm like, 'Oh, shit.' I'm like, 'Where?' He said, 'Philly.' I said, 'You traded him down the street?' So I was just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world." 
You see that little blue cap emoji below Tatum's posted video? That's a response from Brown's account. If you are not fluent in emoji, calling "cap" on something or someone means calling it a lie. 
Now, what Brown was suggesting Tatum was lying about isn't clear, but we can make a pretty safe assumption: Tatum is saying he was caught off guard by the trade, that he didn't know anything about it, and Celtics president Brad Stevens has even said he intentionally kept everyone, including Tatum, in the dark about the deal until it was done. But Brown pretty clearly doesn't believe this. So now we get to Friday night. The Celtics had just beaten the Knicks for their first win of the season, and afterward, Tatum, of course, was asked about Brown's "cap" response to his posted video. Tatum tried to shut it down, saying there is no beef with Brown and that, in essence, the media should stop trying to create one for clicks. "This ain't no f---in' Shaq and Kobe," Tatum said. "There's no beef. It's not about that. It should be more praise [for everything we accomplished together], and I understand that don't necessarily sell. Drama gets clicks and views, but I'm not really -- that's not my thing." 
Which brings us back, finally, to Saturday night, when Brown was asked about Tatum's "no beef" statement and gave us the "lamb chops and gravy" quote that is sure to keep on giving. The mature thing to say about all this, I suppose, is that Brown should move on and quit being so petty and take the high road on which Tatum, a polished pro if there ever was one, is going to continue traveling. I guess I'm not very mature. Don't get me wrong, I don't like writing about this every other day, but I hope it quiets down from that standpoint. I'd rather talk about basketball. But eventually, this will be about basketball. And that's going to be the best part -- when the 76ers host the Celtics on Nov. 10 and then when Brown returns to Boston for the first time on Jan. 21. I don't know about you, but I'm personally praying to the basketball gods that we get a Celtics-Sixers playoff series. Because that's when this little lamb chop would get seriously juicy.

schema.headline: Jaylen Brown refusing to let Jayson Tatum drama die after Celtics-76ers trade - CBS Sports

title: Big 12 CFP picture in chaos: BYU, Texas Tech upset losses alter landscape - CBS Sports
description: Two top-10 titans are unbeaten no more in the Big 12

Two top-10 titans are unbeaten no more in the Big 12

        Hold onto your seats, Big 12 fans.Mid-tier teams in the conference spent Saturday taking a sledgehammer to its own playoff argument following UCF's stunning upset of No. 2 BYU in double overtime and Cincinnati's impressive win over previously-unbeaten and No. 8 Texas Tech.Those results have tossed the conference's College Football Playoff hopes in a blender with Utah being the only unbeaten left entering Week 9.As a result, Utah is now projected as a top-4 in CBS Sports' latest CFP predictions.Cincinnati snapped Texas Tech's nine-game Big 12 winning streak dating back to last season hours before Scott Frost and the Knights held off the Cougars, a week after BYU had beaten Notre Dame to move up to No. 2 in the AP poll. 
With five top-25 teams entering the weekend, the attention now turns to BYU at Utah in a couple of weeks, with the winner getting a leg up on the rest at the top of the conference.Can either of these teams restore order in the unpredictable league standings?Behind four touchdown passes from JC French and a career-best 173 yards rushing from Cole Tabb, Cincinnati snapped a two-game skid with a signature win and took advantage of Texas Tech's season-long sputters in the passing game. Struggles offensively finally came back to haunt the Red Raiders, who turned it over three times and never recovered from Cincinnati's 21-point surge in the second quarter.
The ranked win was only Scott Satterfield's second at Cincinnati in four seasons.It was personal for the Bearcats, who watched last season's starting quarterback, Brendan Sorsby, leave this offseason via the transfer portal to Texas Tech -- though he never played a down for the Red Raiders. Sorsby was suspended following a gambling investigation before mutually parting ways with Texas Tech in June.Now, Will Hammond and the Red Raiders' offense must likely win out — with Arizona looming among others — to have a chance at repeating as Big 12 champions and securing an automatic berth into the CFP.
Top of Big 12 standingsRankTeamOverall RecordConference RecordNo. 10Utah7-04-0No. 2BYU6-13-1No. 8Texas Tech6-13-1No. 25Arizona6-13-1No. 14Houston 6-2 3-2BYU goes down in OrlandoIt's imperative the Big 12's best don't bloody each other up over the second half of the season if this league wants multiple teams in the CFP, especially after BYU's shocking loss at UCF. The selection committee's new conference strength metric helps contextualize league schedules, including disparities between teams with varied schedule difficulty.However, only one of the league's five ranked teams entering Week 8 had a strength of schedule ranked inside the top-35 nationally, and that's going to be part of the discussion when the CFP selection committee meets next weekend. Before Saturday's loss, BYU sat No. 1 in strength of record and No. 7 in game control, metrics that will come in handy if Kalani Sitake's team rebounds as the league favorite.Utah has similar numbers, but the Utes' strength of schedule, at No. 99, is the worst in the conference. That SOS ranking shifted to 89th after Utah exit of Week 8 as the league's lone unbeaten. The Utes also now lead the conference in game control at No. 9 nationally.Neither BYU nor Texas Tech should be written out of the bracket conversation after one disastrous afternoon, but their cushion got thinner and the conference's margin for error followed.Significance of Utah's victoryThe Utes are the last unbeaten remaining in the Big 12 after a wild weekend, giving Utah the upper hand in the CFP discussion and conference title race. Morgan Scalley's squad ended Houston's four-game winning streak Saturday night at Rice-Eccles Stadium in Salt Lake City to move up in sole possession of first in the conference standings.Next week's showdown at Cincinnati could push the Utes closer to the CFP before the Nov. 7 showdown with BYU. From Texas Tech's perspective, the best the Red Raiders can finish is 11-1 overall, and from there, the CFP situation gets interesting for Joey McGuire's team.They'll own the head-to-head advantage over Houston in the event multiple teams end with two conference losses, but the league goes to tiebreakers with common opponents if Utah or BYU are the teams tied with Texas Tech at the end of the regular season. As you can see, the unpredictability within the Big 12 and its quest to produce multiple playoff teams this season will be decided over the next few weekends, but Week 8 results damaged the league's shot at getting three programs in the final bracket.

        A week after logging zero carries, Cam Skattebo is expected to reprise his role as the Giants' lead running back during Sunday's game against the Texans, according to ESPN. The Giants are also expected to work in Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary at various points in the game. New York waived Najee Harris less than 48 hours after last week's loss. "Nobody's safe, it's as simple as that," Skattebo said on Friday of Harris' release. "And I think when we go on the field, and we perform, if we're not performing, we understand there's a possibility of not being here. And if I don't perform, I know there's a possibility of me not being here."  Skattebo's demotion last week came after his fumble in overtime during the Giants' eventual tie against the Commanders. He's lost five fumbles in 13 career games. 
"I got taught a lesson," he said. "I don't know if that's from them or from myself. I had to kind of step back and look at it and figure out why. Why I was doing the things I was doing, what was happening. Came to practice, worked on those things, corrected them. Ready to go back out there and play ball."Skattebo is averaging just 3.6 yards-per-carry this season after he averaged 4.1 yards-per-carry in 2025. He had a successful stretch as the Giants' starting running back last season (he ran for a career-high 98 yards and three scores in a win over the Eagles) before an injury prematurely ended his season. On Sunday, Skattebo will face a Texans defense that has allowed the third-fewest rushing yards in the NFL. Houston's defense is also third in the league in fewest yards-per-carry average allowed. 
The Giants' running game will look to take some of the pressure off of JJ McCarthy, who will make his first start with Big Blue.

title: Steelers' Aaron Rodgers makes history during NFL's first game in Paris - CBS Sports
description: Rodgers continues to make history during his final season
body:
Rodgers continues to make history during his final season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 25, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:43 am ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
            
        
                
                
                
            
        
            
                    
                Getty Images
            
            

    
        Aaron Rodgers has been making history all season, and that continued Sunday in the NFL's first-ever game in Paris. Rodgers became the first quarterback to play in an international game in a different country three straight years. Last year, Rodgers led the Steelers to a win in the first NFL game played in Ireland. In 2024, Rodgers was with the Jets when New York fell to the Vikings in London. Rodgers' second piece of history took place on Pittsburgh's third drive, when he passed Peyton Manning into sole possession of third place on the NFL's all-time regular season passing touchdown list. Rodgers passed Manning on the career touchdown pass list during the Steelers' Week 5 win over the Colts. 
The record-setting touchdown pass -- the 540th of his career -- was a four-yard completion to Darnell Washington, Pittsburgh's massive tight end who has become a Rodgers favorite. 
The 42-year-old, four-time league MVP has been enjoying a successful season with the Steelers, who are in pursuit of their 23rd consecutive non-losing season. He recently became the first Steelers quarterback since Terry Bradshaw to throw three touchdown passes in three straight games. Rodgers has also thrown multiple touchdown passes in four straight games for the first time since 2022, his final season with the Packers. 
Earlier this season, Rodgers passed former Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger for fifth all-time in regular season wins by a starting quarterback. Barring injury, he should pass Drew Brees for fourth all-time by season's end.

title: Inter Miami's MLS Cup hopes take hit with problems too big for Lionel Messi to solve - CBS Sports
description: HARRISON, N.J. – The sun was beginning to set as thousands clad in pink jerseys settled into their seats, hoping to see a show. The wait
body:
HARRISON, N.J. – The sun was beginning to set as thousands clad in pink jerseys settled into their seats, hoping to see a show. The wait was not particularly long – with Lionel Messi temporarily a member of a captive audience, 17-year-old midfielder Adri Mehmeti made World Cup winner Rodrigo de Paul march to the beat of his drum. Red Bull New York were up on reigning MLS Cup champions Inter Miami seconds later thanks to a Casemiro own goal, the lead fully deserved.
A moment of brilliance from a rising local star is now a weekly occurrence in MLS, especially from those who took part in the U.S. men's national team's generational shift-themed friendlies this fall. It was perhaps one of few guarantees on Saturday, the main one being Messi's presence. He was the reason, after all, that Sports Illustrated Stadium was actually full, this time with spectators who jumped out of concession lines in the 56th minute to see Messi enter the pitch. He's the person whose name is chanted more often than any of the home team's players by a very healthy margin, no matter the MLS stadium. It's the kind of request Inter Miami always feel obliged to grant because of his inexplicable excellence, even if he was in Oviedo, Spain, two days earlier to accept the Princess of Asturias award for sport. The appetite for Messi is insatiable in that way, to the point that the vast majority of people in the building believed he would flip the game on its head in a single moment.It never happened.Miami fell flat in a 2-0 defeat to the Red Bulls, who precariously sit in the final playoff position with three games to go. The 16 points and six places that separate them in the Eastern Conference indicated that Miami would at least assert themselves at times on Saturday, but they failed to make a dent in more ways than one. Mehmeti's ability to outperform De Paul for the game's opening goal set the tone for the evening in a lot of ways, losing the game as soon as they lost the midfield battle. It was not that they lacked the opportunity to impose themselves – they had 65.9% possession, took 906 touches and completed 86.3% of their 714 passes. That possession never translated to an actual ability to dominate the game, their performance disjointed and ineffective in the end."Our build-up play from the back was slow, and we lost possession in areas where we simply cannot afford to lose the ball," Miami head coach Cristian "Kily" Gonzalez said post-match. "Because of these turnovers — whether due to poor passing, bad touches, or other errors — we ended up being caught too spread out as a team. I don't want to take any credit away from our opponent, but I believe the main issue was our own failure to maintain the style of play that defines us — specifically, avoiding so many turnovers in the midfield. We were also caught out by passes played behind our lines and we weren't compact enough. We improved a little bit after halftime, but I'm certainly not satisfied. We're in a phase where we cannot afford to relax — not even for a moment — or else we'll face serious consequences. We weren't the best team before, and we certainly aren't the worst now; we just need to get back to our usual way of playing and regain our rhythm."
The Red Bulls are hardly the team one would expect to exploit Miami's weaknesses, notably ineffective in their own way. The 2-0 scoreline was generous to Miami, the hosts wasteful with 19 shots and 3.24 expected goals, the likes of Julian Hall and Jorge Ruvalcaba missing sitter after sitter. It is not much of a surprise for a team that ranks inside MLS' top five for expected goals with 57.02 but has just 41 goals to show for it but even then, they succeeded fully in exploiting Miami's weaknesses. Mehmeti's outing, one of the best of his young career, was the foundation for a Red Bulls performance, particularly in a dominant first half."Honestly, the maturity he has is unbelievable," the Red Bulls' Mohammed Sofo said. "The vision he has – he knows when to play for it, when to come down. Sometimes he does things, I'm like, 'Wow.' For me as a No. 8 or also as a No. 10, I try to find myself in the pockets and sometimes he finds me with just two touches. Other players need to take a first touch, look for it and then play but for him, from the second touch, he finds you."Mehmeti's excellence allowed the Red Bulls to survive even once Messi entered the game.
"We all know how good he is," Red Bulls coach Michael Bradley said. "We all know how special he is. I said last week, for me, he's the best player of all time but I also know that you don't want to let really good players just do whatever they want and to just back off and admire the qualities, that doesn't get you what you want so you know that he's going to be able to twist and turn and dribble through tight spaces and find his way out of a certain spot. You know that he's going to be able to play certain passes but we still talked and worked all week on the idea of making the game really hard, not just on Miami but on Messi in particular and again in the middle of all that, there's still going to be certain plays but we wanted the first guy ready to close down and take away the direct path to goal. We wanted the second guy coming ready every single time on the inside. We wanted in certain moments a third guy ready, close and so that part was generally good when he came on and so I was more pleased with that part."Messi, of course, did what he could to help Miami but at 39 years old and after two transatlantic flights in a handful of days, the spark was not there. He was hardly at his freshest, generating 0.13 expected goals plus expected assists and creating two chances along the way. Miami looked a bit better as a whole after his arrival, generating 0.51 expected goals from five shots. It was technically an improvement from the 0.3 expected goals they mustered in the 55 minutes before Messi's substitution but for a title-contending team, the results were not impressive in the slightest.This, of course, is not Messi's fault. He is the perfect, and perhaps only, player a team can build an entire strategy around. Even on the days where he is mostly absent, he can still turn up – only three months have passed since Messi was kept at bay in a World Cup semifinal for 85 minutes, only to notch two assists and send Argentina to the final. It is genuinely worth asking if that approach is actually a sustainable one, though. There was only going to be so much gas in the tank of a team fueled by Messi – and for that matter, Luis Suarez – in the final years of their careers. Miami won MLS Cup last year with their help but also with an actual plan by ex-head coach Javier Mascherano, who was out of a job four months later.
Gonzalez, who had a 32.5% win percentage in a coaching career that had only consisted of jobs in Argentina before Miami hired him in late summer, has not found the solutions to Miami's problems. If three wins in seven games was not enough for Mascherano to keep his job, Gonzalez's identical record is not much better. Miami, though, look more aimless now than they have since Messi joined the club three years ago and are running out of time for Gonzalez to fix it before the playoffs begin next month.In a team sport, Miami's problems might just be too big for Messi to solve all by himself.Mehmeti's breakout season continuesWhile fans fill stadiums to see the likes of Messi, LAFC's Son Heung-min and the Chicago Fire's Robert Lewandowski, they are often treated to something else entirely these days – a teenager doing what he can to leave a strong impression. Mehmeti did just that on Saturday, an appropriate feat for a freshly-capped USMNT player who has been the talk of MLS sporting executives for some time. Bradley was quick to remind, though, that his quick rise is impressive even if his potential was easy to spot.
"He has personality," Bradley said. "He has technical ability, the technical ability that you need to play in that spot in the center of the field when spaces are tight and things happen fast. He has a feel and an understanding for the game and obviously, the way things have gone this year, we've thrown an incredible amount at him. I've also said this a bunch of times. I didn't know coming into the season what exactly it was going to mean for Adri, or Julian, or Matty dos Santos, or any of our young guys. We knew that they were going to be a real part of the first team and in the end, it was going to be we were going to see how things played out, how they responded every day, how they took to ideas, how they pushed themselves along in the group, how they earned respect and the way it has gone means that we have put a lot on Adri's plate. We expect a lot of him. He has a lot of responsibility in our team for a 17-year-old, and he doesn't bat an eye."Mehmeti's strong outing against Miami came after two games where he was substituted off before the hour mark, all on the back of a first camp with the U.S. team where his international teammates popped off more than he did. Growth is hardly linear, though, especially for a 17-year-old in the midst of his first season as a professional."Are there things that need to continue to improve? Yeah, absolutely," Bradley said. "Have there been certain games where, for this reason or that reason, we end up feeling like no, tonight's a night where we got to make a change and get him off a little bit earlier? Yeah, there have been but generally speaking, when you talk about a 17-year-old kid who has played in that spot on our team and when you think about the way that we play and what gets asked of him in that role, he's doing really well."
Mehmeti's settings are ideal as he continues to chart an upward trajectory. USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino has described MLS as a strong place for young players to begin their professional careers, while Bradley himself will have plenty of insight to offer Mehmeti. The Red Bulls head coach was once the celebrated midfield engine of the USMNT, the former national team captain winning 151 caps and playing in two World Cups during his career."I just think the full package has improved in every way," he said about Mehmeti's progress this season. "He has taken the qualities that he has and has made them hold up as games get better and harder and faster and as opponents get that much better and within that, there are little things that need to continue to get better. We've talked a little bit lately about his understanding in certain situations when we can't be aggressive or when it's not a real counter-pressing moment and he has to then slide out a little bit on an angle and deal with an attack or just his understanding of how to take a good angle and make sure that he can control that situation so it doesn't turn into anything more dangerous and so as I said, these are all normal things that when you're a young player playing in that position and there is that much responsibility, you have to live it. You have to play through it. You have to make certain mistakes so that you understand, 'I can't do that exactly the same way again,' and so he's moving himself forward in a really good way."

title: 2026 World Series: How Sal Frelick became unlikely Brewers hero with Game 2 homer - CBS Sports
description: Frelick delivered the swing of his life, a tying sixth-inning homer, as Milwaukee completed yet another postseaso
body:
Frelick delivered the swing of his life, a tying sixth-inning homer, as Milwaukee completed yet another postseason comeback
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 25, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:10 am ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        MILWAUKEE -- Ian Seymour kept testing Sal Frelick late Saturday night, almost dismissive of what the Brewers outfielder might be capable of producing.But Frelick has never been one to shrink when his mettle is challenged. His competitive fire only burns hotter.In the bottom of the sixth inning in Game 2 of the World Series, with the Brewers on the brink of erasing a four-run deficit for the second time this postseason, the lefthanded Rays reliever kept feeding Frelick fastballs.All nine pitches of the at-bat, in fact. Alternating between two variations of the pitch for much of it. 
Sinker. Four-seam. Sinker. Four-seam. Sinker. Four-seam. Sinker. Four-seam."I'm an eight-hole hitter," Frelick said, detailing the number of fastballs he saw. "I'm a lefty. You have to assume a guy like that is coming at you."Frelick kept fighting, just as he had his whole career. He fouled off half of the first eight pitches he saw and ultimately worked the count full.Seymour became predictable, a creature of habit, not doubling up on the same pitch twice to that point. 
That was until the ninth pitch of the at-bat.Seymour tested Frelick again, throwing a four-seamer for the second consecutive pitch, this one hanging over the inner third of the plate. Frelick didn't miss it, crushing a solo shot to tie the score at four apiece.
Bedlam ensued at American Family Field. Yellow towels twirled in unison throughout the stands. And as the stadium erupted, so did Frelick, rounding first base. He pointed toward his bullpen. They pointed back. Because for these Brewers, deficits have become invitations. Adversity only fuels the congregation.Winning feels inevitable, as Milwaukee's 5-4 victory in Game 2 demonstrated.Frelick, who'd hit just four regular-season home runs, didn't deliver the final blow. Cooper Pratt did. Yet he made certain the Brewers would have the chance to land it.
"He hit four lasers tonight," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. "He hit four balls right on the screws. We talked about it in pregame, he's got the 'it factor.'" The "it factor" that Murphy sees in Frelick was forged on the high school football field, where he earned Massachusetts Gatorade Player of the Year honors as a quarterback in 2017.The "it factor" was cultivated on ice skates, in a state where hockey borders on religion.
The "it factor" was instilled by his father, Jeff, who played football at the University of Pittsburgh before injuries cut his career short.The "it factor" was fortified through doubt. For all his accolades, Frelick still had to fight to be seen. At just 5-foot-8, he was accustomed to being overlooked."Everybody's built differently," Murphy said. "Everybody expresses it differently. I think that Sal was a young man that had very good physical skills, but he wasn't big in stature like a lot of these guys are. So, as a smaller guy, I think he always was having to prove how great he was. He has this edge about him that he believes in himself."

        
            
                Aaron Ashby on the verge of MLB history as Brewers reliever continues dominant postseason run
                
                    Matt Snyder                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
It's an edge Murphy likened to longtime Red Sox second baseman Dustin Pedroia, whom he coached at Arizona State. Pedroia possessed physical gifts Frelick doesn't, but both share an insatiable desire to dominate, regardless of what their natural abilities suggest."Murph will tell you firsthand that it's never pretty watching me take a swing or run or field or whatever it might be," Frelick said. "I just always felt like that was where I was able to get my edge was just kind of turn everything into a competition. Put myself in the box and iso me and the pitcher. Or on defense, just iso me and the ball. How can I beat it?"Maybe not the prettiest swing, but the prettiest of outcomes. A reminder of how October has a way of washing away the tribulations endured just to get there. How an entire regular season can be reduced to a footnote when a player delivers in the postseason.
Because Frelick's regular season was anything but memorable. He hit just .230 with a .614 OPS.A right shoulder injury sidelined him for six weeks, costing him half of July and most of August. And when he returned, his role had diminished. Though the Brewers have long embraced platoons, Frelick found himself largely relegated to facing right-handed pitching.
Luis Lara, the 21-year-old prospect called up in July, had taken some of Frelick's playing time down the stretch. But Frelick didn't sulk. His focus only sharpened. His emotions, rarely on display, are encased in steel. He can take tough coaching.
In May, Murphy acknowledged he didn't tell Frelick he loved him enough. So he scribbled himself a reminder: Tell Sal, "I love you, Sal."Then he thought better of it. Crossed it out."You know what? He doesn't need me to tell him that," Murphy said.Beneath the humor was a truth: Frelick doesn't need constant reassurance. His competitiveness, his confidence, his unwavering sense of self -- all nurtured over time."It was great," Frelick said of his home run. "Like, sort of this blackout feeling. Then it kind of ends. We were tied. We weren't winning or anything."
The Brewers now have a chance to capture the first World Series championship in franchise history as the series shifts to Tropicana Field, where the Rays have been dominant, going 59-27 this season, including the postseason.It will be another test for Milwaukee in a series decided by one run in the first two games. The Rays won't go quietly.Yet at every turn, Milwaukee has answered the challenge.And on Saturday night, Frelick answered his.Because as leaves fall and flowers wilt, Frelick has bloomed.
